chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Abu al-Qasim al-Sayqal, who said:
I wrote to him saying: 'I am a sword-polisher; I buy swords and sell them to the Sultan. Is it permissible for me to sell them?' He wrote back in peace: 'There is no harm in it.'

key_terms.الصَّيْقَلِ: A polisher or finisher, specifically of swords or metal
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no harm in it (a common legal ruling indicating permissibility)

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a craftsman to sell weapons to the government or ruler in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, the sword-polisher al-Sayqal seeks clarification from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) regarding the permissibility of selling swords to the Sultan, reflecting the practical economic realities of the Shia community under various ruling powers. The Imam’s concise response, 'There is no harm in it' (La ba'sa bihi), establishes a baseline of permissibility for this trade, distinguishing it from sales to enemies in times of war or specific prohibitions on direct use in oppression. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly approach of evaluating the context of the buyer and the end-use of goods rather than imposing a blanket prohibition on artisans' trades.
